Hello voat community of linux from newbie to both.

Looking for HW Monitor alternative to make sure my OC'd CPU is not overheating, searching the web lm-sensors been the only one I could find and it does not take logs like HW Monitor, please if there is any other let me know.

Kind regards, Thanks.

lm-sensors does have logging, "sensord" daemon makes logs and is part of the lm_sensors project. Looking for alternatives may not go far, as the sensor drivers are mostly generic but most likely untested for anything other than lm_sensors. sensord will log sensors every how many seconds you wish.

As for overheating, while I am not certain of which cpu/motherboard/linux-kernel/bios-option combination you have, Linux in general will avoid overclocking. If the default power manager is run, it'll frequently turn off overclocking. Assuming you have a bios that makes enough information available to Linux to avoid it's cautious default of stock clock speeds, very few boards should be allowed to overheat. As long as cpu throttling hasn't been disabled, there are still several defaults to change to allow overheating. To overheat a chip, bios would need to set the clock to OC, Linux would have to have monitoring and power management turned off, and bios would have to have thermal throttling disabled... then perhaps it could overheat.

Most importantly, does your chip really need to be OC'd? There are certainty games and multimedia applications than can be use every bit of cpu thrown at them... but most application on Linux are fairly well tuned to still work fine on slow processors (anything in last decade or so). While OC does make sense when Windows spins the hourglass for several minutes double checking, its double check, of the redundant check, of the last update... slow... My personal Linux box is most often slowed down by disk access. There are numerous tips, tricks and speed hacks for storage, which will cause a much greater increase in usability. Mostly just get SSD and cram as much of the system into cache as possible. look up preload and prelink for tuning starters.

Seems you already got some good answers, but here's my two cents.

As you already know, the lm-sensors program lets you view temperatures. If you are on a debian based distribution (ubuntu, mint, etc), install it with sudo apt-get install lm-sensors

After install, you will run this from a shell by executing sensors command.

Furthermore, you can install (or it might already be) the watch program, that will run a specified command once every X seconds: watch -n 1 sensors shows you temperatures updated every second.
